Bio: Quasimodo was a French bell-ringer who spent his entire life in near-total seclusion within the towers of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris. Born with severe physical deformities—including a pronounced spinal curvature, restricted mobility, and a facial tumor—he was abandoned as an infant on the church steps and raised by the cathedral's archdeacon, Claude Frollo. The deafening roar of the massive cathedral bells eventually left him completely deaf, compounding his isolation from Parisian society, which frequently subjected him to cruelty and public humiliation. Despite a life defined by intense loneliness and marginalization, those close to him noted his fierce loyalty and profound capacity for empathy, most notably demonstrated in his protective devotion to a young local woman named Esmeralda. He passed away shortly after her tragic death, leaving behind a legacy as one of the most enduring symbols of inner humanity and resilience in French cultural history.

Baldwin IV (1161–1185), known as the Leper King, was the king of Jerusalem from 1174 until his death in 1185. Baldwin ascended to the throne when he was thirteen despite having leprosy. He made several attempts to curb the increasing power of the Muslim ruler Saladin, though much of his life was marked by infighting amongst the kingdom's nobles. Throughout his reign, and especially at the end of his brief life, he was troubled by his succession, working to select a suitable heir to the throne and prevent a succession crisis. Choosing competent advisers, Baldwin ruled a thriving crusader state, protecting it from Saladin.

Judas Iscariot was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus Christ, living during the first century AD. Little is known about his early life, but the Gospels describe him as a close follower who traveled with Jesus and managed the disciples' shared money. He later betrayed Jesus to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver, identifying him with a kiss in the Garden of Gethsemane and enabling his arrest. According to Matthew's Gospel, Judas was overcome with remorse, returned the silver, and took his own life. Once a trusted companion, he became one of history's most enduring symbols of betrayal.

Lucius Domitius Aurelianus (c. 214 – 275 AD) was Roman emperor from 270 to 275, during the Crisis of the Third Century. Rising through the ranks of the army, he reunited a fracturing empire: he crushed the Palmyrene Empire of Zenobia in the east and reclaimed the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, earning the title Restitutor Orbis, 'Restorer of the World.' He drove the Goths and Vandals back across the Danube, reformed the debased currency, and ringed the capital with the great Aurelian Walls that still stand today. His brief but decisive reign ended when he was assassinated by his own officers while campaigning in the east.

Sigismund of Luxembourg (1368-1437) was Holy Roman Emperor from 1433 and King of Bohemia from 1419. He was crowned King of Bohemia in Prague, and spent much of his reign trying to hold that kingdom, Hungary, and the empire together. He called the Council of Constance and fought the Hussite wars in Bohemia.

Philip II Augustus (1165-1223) was King of France from 1180. He made Paris the true capital of the kingdom, paved its main streets, built the wall around the growing city, and raised the Louvre as a fortress. He broke the Angevin hold on Normandy and left France the strongest kingdom in western Europe.

Kublai Khan (1215-1294), grandson of Genghis Khan, founded China's Yuan dynasty. He conquered the Song and established his capital at Dadu, the city that became Beijing. From that court he ruled the largest of the Mongol realms and opened it to traders and envoys from across Eurasia.

Frederick II of Prussia (1712-1786), called Frederick the Great, was king from 1740 and ruled from Berlin. He enlarged Prussia through war and reform, patronized music and philosophy, and turned Berlin into a capital of the European Enlightenment.

Emperor Guangwu of Han (5 BC-AD 57), born Liu Xiu, restored the Han dynasty after the collapse of Wang Mang's Xin regime. He took the throne in AD 25 and made Luoyang his eastern capital. His reign began the Eastern Han and steadied China after years of civil war.
Maria Theresa (1717-1780), Habsburg Empress who ruled from Vienna, modernizing the empire and transforming the city into a cultural hub.

Pericles (c. 495-429 BC) led Athens through its golden age. As strategos he directed the Delian League, sponsored the Parthenon and the other buildings of the Acropolis, and made Athens the cultural center of the Greek world. He died of the plague during the Peloponnesian War.

Baybars (c. 1223-1277) was the Mamluk sultan of Egypt and Syria and ruled from Cairo. A former soldier, he stopped the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut and took the remaining crusader strongholds of the Levant. He strengthened Cairo and left the Mamluk state the major power of the eastern Mediterranean.
Poseidon, Greek god of the sea, earthquakes, and horses, who stirs or calms the waves with his trident. In Plato's account the island of Atlantis was his allotted realm.
Mansa of the Mali Empire, whose 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca displayed the wealth of West Africa.

Queen of Palmyra who ruled Syria and led her own armies against Rome.

Medieval queen of Georgia whose reign is remembered as a golden age of that kingdom.

Persian scholar in Baghdad whose algebra and astronomical tables shaped later mathematics.
Moroccan traveler of the fourteenth century whose Rihla records decades of journeys across Africa and Asia.
The only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name, during the Tang and Zhou years.
Founder of the al-Qarawiyyin mosque and university in Fez in the ninth century.

Japanese daimyo who began the unification of Japan in the late sixteenth century.

King of Wessex who held England against the Great Heathen Army and backed laws, burhs, and learning.
Carian queen who commanded ships for Xerxes at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BC.

Bio: Seventeenth-century Mexican Hieronymite nun and poet who argued for women's right to study.
Pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, known for Abu Simbel and his claimed victory at Kadesh.

Last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, remembered for her reign in Alexandria and her alliances with Rome.
Chinese teacher whose sayings, gathered in the Analects, shaped ethics and government in East Asia.
Chinese sage traditionally credited with the Dao De Jing and the beginnings of Daoist thought.
English mathematician whose notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine include the first published computer algorithm.
Byzantine emperor whose long reign defeated Bulgaria and left the imperial treasury full.
Mughal empress who shared Jahangir's rule and issued imperial orders in her own name.
Kandake of Kush who fought Roman Egypt, known from Strabo's account of the Kushite raid on Syene.
